opus-5.5.text:
Guest: I think the simplest way to see it is that the number of people on the internet has a ceiling, but the number of agents doesn't. Human search demand is bounded by how many people there are, how many hours they have, and how much they're willing to type into a box. Once you have agents doing work on someone's behalf, those limits go away.

When a person researches something, they might run a few queries, skim some results, and stop because they're tired or it's good enough. An agent doing the same task doesn't get tired. It can run dozens or hundreds of queries, read far more pages, cross-check sources, and go back for more when it finds a gap. So for a single human intent, you get a large multiplier in the number of times the web gets queried.

Then you multiply again by the number of agents. Each person might have many agents running in the background: monitoring something, doing research, comparing options, keeping information current. A lot of that work isn't even triggered by a person in the moment. It runs continuously. So I expect the web to be used far more by agents than by people, and the gap to keep growing.

That changes what search needs to be. Search engines for humans were built around ten blue links, ads, and a person who reads the page. An agent wants something else. It wants high-recall results, the actual content rather than a link to click, the ability to go deep on a long-tail query, and predictable cost and latency because it's making so many calls. It also needs good information about freshness and provenance, because it has to reason about whether to trust what it finds.

So the opportunity isn't just "more searches." It's a different kind of customer with different needs, and that customer will end up doing most of the searching. I think the infrastructure for that, meaning how you index the web, how you rank for a machine reader, and how you price it, has to be rebuilt with agents as the main user. That's the bet we're making.

r001.rationale: The response says an agent can issue dozens or hundreds of queries for a task, but does not state that it can do so while answering within a few seconds.

r002.rationale: It describes many agents running background tasks, but does not identify developer-programmed workflows or compare their multiplier with individual assistant interactions.

r003.rationale: It contrasts a person researching and stopping with an agent doing the same work continuously in the background, conveying that automating the process enables it to run more often and increase searches.

fable-5.1.text:
The way I think about it is that search, for most of its history, has been bounded by human attention. A person has a question, they type it in, they look at a page of results, and that's the end of the transaction. The number of searches in the world was roughly a function of how many people there were and how many moments of curiosity they had in a day. That constraint is going away.

When an agent is working on a task for you, it doesn't do one search. It does dozens, sometimes hundreds. It searches, reads, realizes it needs to verify something, searches again, cross-references, goes down a branch that turns out to be a dead end, comes back. A single question from a person can fan out into an entire research session that no human would ever have had the patience to do themselves. So the demand isn't just growing, it's changing shape. It's becoming bursty, deep, and recursive in a way that the old model of search was never designed for.

And the thing I find most interesting is that the consumer of the result is different. A person wants ten blue links and a nice interface. An agent wants the actual content, in a form it can reason over, with enough context to judge whether a source is trustworthy. It doesn't care about ads, it doesn't care about layout. So the product you have to build for that demand looks very different from what we've all been using for twenty years. It's much more like infrastructure, something that sits underneath and feeds models what they need to think with.

I'd also say we're early. Most of the agent traffic today is still fairly simple retrieval. But as models get better at planning and persisting over long tasks, the number of searches per human intent is going to keep climbing. I genuinely think that within a few years, the majority of search volume on the internet won't be initiated by a person typing into a box. It'll be machines doing work on people's behalf. That's a pretty profound shift for anyone who cares about how information moves.

r001.rationale: The response says an agent may run dozens or hundreds of searches for a task, but does not establish that it can do so within a few seconds.

r002.rationale: It discusses agents expanding searches per human intent, but does not identify developer-programmed workflows as a larger demand multiplier than individual assistant interactions.

r003.rationale: It describes searches branching and recurring during an agent task, but does not explain that automating a manual process increases demand by letting that process run more frequently.

astra-6.text:
I think the big change is that a search becomes an intermediate step in doing something, rather than something a person explicitly initiates. You might ask an agent to research a topic or help you make a decision. To complete that task, it may need to search, read what it finds, identify gaps, and search again. One request from you can turn into many requests for information.

And as agents can handle longer, more complex tasks, that information need grows. So search demand becomes tied to how much work agents are doing, not just how many people are sitting in front of a search box.

That also changes what makes search useful. The agent needs information that helps it take the next step, with enough context to assess whether it can trust it. The opportunity is both serving more searches and making those searches useful to a different kind of consumer.

r001.rationale: It says one user request can lead to repeated searches, but does not state that an agent can issue them within a few seconds.

r002.rationale: It does not identify developer-programmed workflows or compare their demand multiplier with individual assistant interactions.

r003.rationale: It does not explain that automating a manual process can make it run more often and thereby increase search demand.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the way to think about it is that human attention is no longer the only constraint on search demand. Today, a person asks a question, looks at a few results, and decides what to do. An agent can take that same question and break it into many smaller questions, search for each of them, compare sources, and come back with an answer.

So one human request might generate dozens of searches behind the scenes. And as agents take on longer tasks, they’ll need to retrieve information at multiple steps, because the world changes and the model doesn’t know everything.

The interesting shift is that search becomes less about presenting a page of links and more about supplying the right information to another system. That puts a lot of emphasis on relevance, freshness, latency, and cost. The demand could grow substantially, but serving that demand well requires thinking about search as infrastructure for agents.
